concepts.definition: Words that replace nouns as the subject of a sentence
concepts.example: 9 essential words: I, you, he, she, we, you (formal), they (masc), they (fem), {on}

concepts.definition: 4 singular pronouns (one person) and 4 plural pronouns (multiple people)

concepts.definition: French has TWO words for "you" - informal (friends) and formal (strangers/bosses)

concepts.definition: The most common way to say 'we' in French - more natural than '{nous}'
concepts.example: {On} means 'we' when friends talk, or 'people' in general. It takes the same verb form as {il} and {elle}.

concepts.definition: The most important verb. Describes states and identity.
concepts.example: Express: I am, you are, he is, she is, we are, they are

concepts.definition: Each pronoun gets a unique verb form - you must memorize all 8 to communicate who is doing what!
concepts.example: {je suis}, {tu es}, {il est}, {elle est}, {nous sommes}, {vous êtes}, {ils sont}, {elles sont}

concepts.definition: Use it with an adjective, as in "I am happy", or with your name, as in "I am Paul".
concepts.example: {Je suis heureux} (I am happy), {Il est heureux} (he is happy), {Je suis Paul} (I am Paul), {Tu es bon !} (you're good!)

concepts.definition: With the words from the first lesson, you can already answer a waiter.
concepts.example: {Bonjour ! Café ?} (Hello! Coffee?) {Oui, merci !} (Yes, thanks!)

concepts.definition: You can NEVER say a noun alone in French - must use an article!
concepts.example: English: 'book', French: MUST say 'a book' or 'the book'

concepts.definition: un (masculine), une (feminine) = a/an
concepts.example: Use when talking about any one thing, not a specific thing

concepts.definition: le (masculine), la (feminine), les (plural) = the
concepts.example: Use when talking about a specific thing

concepts.definition: Article must match the noun's gender - this is critical!
concepts.example: Masculine nouns use un/le, feminine nouns use une/{la}

concepts.definition: Every French noun is either masculine or feminine - you must memorize this!
concepts.example: Masculine nouns use '{le/un}', feminine use 'la/{une'}

concepts.definition: Combine nouns with {être} and {avoir}, the verbs you already know
concepts.example: Pattern: pronoun + verb + article + noun

concepts.definition: Every exercise uses être or avoir - reinforcing what you learned!
concepts.example: Learn nouns WHILE practicing your verbs

concepts.definition: When you identify someone with a noun (like 'man' or 'friend'), you MUST use an article (un, une). NOTE: A special rule for professions and nationalities will be taught later.
concepts.example: Correct for now: '{elle est une amie}'. Future rule: '{elle est avocate}' (she is a lawyer).

concepts.definition: Essential irregular verb for expressing desires and polite requests! One of the most common verbs in French.

concepts.term: Three Ways to Ask Questions in French
concepts.definition: French has 3 methods for asking questions. Start with the easiest!
concepts.example: 1) {Est-ce que} (easiest), 2) Intonation (informal), 3) Inversion (formal)

concepts.definition: Add '{est-ce que}' before ANY statement to make it a question. No word order change needed!
concepts.example: Statement: '{tu as un chat}' → Question: '{est-ce que tu as un chat?}' (do you have a cat?)

concepts.definition: Put question word first, then '{est-ce que}', then statement
concepts.example: {où est-ce que tu es?} (where are you?), {quand est-ce que tu as le livre?} (when do you have the book?)

concepts.definition: Just say a statement with rising voice at the end - super informal!
concepts.example: {Tu as un chat? ↗} (you have a cat?), {Tu es où? ↗} (you are where?)

concepts.definition: Flip verb and subject, add hyphen. Used in formal/written French
concepts.example: {As-tu un chat?} (have you a cat?), {Où es-tu?} (where are you?)

concepts.definition: These words unlock every question you need: what, who, where, when, how, why, how much
concepts.example: {que}/{quoi} (what), {qui} (who), {où} (where), {quand} (when), {comment} (how), {pourquoi} (why), {combien} (how much/many)

concepts.definition: '{Que}' starts questions, '{quoi}' ends them or stands alone
concepts.example: {Que veux-tu?} (what do you want?) vs {Tu veux quoi?} (you want what?) vs {Quoi?} (what?!)

concepts.definition: Some questions are used so often they become fixed phrases
concepts.example: {qu'est-ce que c'est?} (what is it?), {comment ça va?} (how's it going?), {ça va?} (you good?), {qu'est-ce que tu veux?} (what do you want?), {est-ce que tu peux?} (can you?)

parts/p-flip-the-verb.heading: Flip the verb
text: For formal speech and writing, put the verb before the subject and join them with a hyphen. This is called inversion.
parts/p-flip-the-verb.note: You will see it in books, formal emails and the news.

parts/p-raise-your-voice.heading: Raise your voice
text: In everyday speech, French speakers often keep the statement as it is and raise their voice at the end.
parts/p-raise-your-voice.note: Same words, different tone. This is how friends talk to each other.

concepts.definition: Express doing something DESPITE another condition
concepts.example: {Bien que je sois fatigué, je travaille} (Although I'm tired, I'm working), {Bien que je sois fatigué, je t'aide pour que tu partes avant qu'il soit trop tard} (Although I'm tired, I'm helping you so you can leave before it's too late)

concepts.definition: Doing something despite obstacles - shows perseverance!
concepts.example: {Bien qu'il fasse froid, on va au parc} (Even though it's cold, we're going to the park)

concepts.definition: Use to talk about timing relative to someone else's action
concepts.example: {Avant que tu partes} (Before you leave), {Avant qu'il arrive} (Before he arrives)

concepts.definition: Coordinating actions, giving warnings, setting deadlines
concepts.example: {Finis avant que papa rentre!} (Finish before dad gets home!), {Avant que tu partes, parlons en mangeant} (Before you leave, let's talk while we eat)

concepts.definition: French uses different verb forms after phrases like '{il faut que}' (someone needs to), '{je veux que}' (I want someone to), '{je suis content que}' (I'm happy that someone...). These express wishes, needs, or emotions about OTHER PEOPLE's actions.
concepts.example: Normal statement: {Tu es gentil} (You are kind). Wish about you: {Il faut que tu sois gentil} (You need to be kind - different form!)

concepts.term: Where You CAN Use These Forms
concepts.definition: ONLY after certain phrases: il faut que, je veux que, je suis content que, j'ai peur que, avant que, pour que, bien que, etc.
concepts.example: ✓ {Il faut que tu sois gentil} (You need to be kind), ✓ {Je veux qu'il aille} (I want him to go)

concepts.term: Where You CANNOT Use These Forms
concepts.definition: DON'T use these for normal statements, questions, or with just il faut/je veux (no '{que}')
concepts.example: ✗ {Tu sois content?} (Wrong! Say: {Tu es content?}). ✗ {Il faut aller} (Correct - no '{que}' = normal form)

concepts.definition: If you see '{que}' + a person after these starter phrases, use these forms!
concepts.example: {il faut QUE tu} → use sois/{aies}/{ailles}/{fasses, je veux QUE tu} → use sois/aies/ailles/{fasses}

concepts.example: {du chat} (of the cat), {de la maison} (of the house), {des livres} (of the books)

concepts.definition: à + le = au, à + les = aux (but à + la stays separate!)

concepts.definition: Use du/de la/de l'/des to mean 'some' (unspecified quantity)

concepts.definition: de + l' and à + l' before vowel sounds (no contraction needed)

parts/p-the-silent-ent.heading: The silent -ent
text: For {ils} and {elles}, the verb ends in -ent.
parts/p-the-silent-ent.note: The -ent is written but not spoken. In writing, it tells you that several people are doing something. It can change how the letters before it sound, so {ils veulent} sounds a little different from {il veut}.

concepts.definition: Words that show ownership and go directly before the noun they modify
concepts.example: 15 total forms: MY ({mon}/{ma}/{mes}), YOUR informal ({ton}/{ta}/{tes}), HIS/HER ({son}/{sa}/{ses}), OUR ({notre}/{nos}), YOUR formal ({votre}/{vos}), THEIR ({leur}/{leurs})

concepts.term: 🔑 CRITICAL RULE: Agreement with the THING owned
concepts.definition: The possessive adjective matches the gender/number of the THING being owned, NOT the owner
concepts.example: Marie's book = {SON livre} (masculine '{son}' because '{livre}' is masculine, even though Marie is female). Pierre's house = {SA maison} (feminine '{sa}' because '{maison}' is feminine, even though Pierre is male)

concepts.definition: French has two ways to say 'your' depending on relationship and respect level
concepts.example: INFORMAL with friends/family: {ton}/{ta}/{tes} ({ton ami}, {ta maison}, {tes livres}). FORMAL with strangers/respect: {votre}/{vos} ({votre maison}, {vos amis})

concepts.definition: Some possessives don't change for masculine/feminine - only for singular/plural
concepts.example: {NOTRE}/{NOS} (our): {notre maison}, {notre ami}, {nos enfants. VOTRE}/{VOS} (your formal): {votre livre}, {votre famille}, {vos idées. LEUR}/{LEURS} (their): {leur chat}, {leur maison}, {leurs amis}

concepts.definition: Each owner has a predictable number of forms to memorize
concepts.example: MY, YOUR (informal), HIS/HER = 3 forms each (masc/fem/plural). OUR, YOUR (formal), THEIR = 2 forms each (singular/plural only)

concepts.example: {le nord} (north), {le sud} (south), {l'est} (east), {l'ouest} (west)

concepts.definition: Essential for giving and following directions
concepts.example: {tournez à gauche} (turn left), {tournez à droite} (turn right), {tout droit} (straight ahead)

concepts.definition: Describe where things are relative to other things
concepts.example: {à côté de} (next to), {en face de} (across from), {près de} (near), {loin de} (far from)

concepts.definition: Complete phrases for helping someone navigate

concepts.definition: How to ask for help when lost

concepts.definition: One of the most common verbs - used for gifts, help, information, objects
concepts.example: {Je donne un livre} (I give a book), {Tu me donnes ton numéro?} (Do you give me your number?)

concepts.definition: Follows standard -ER pattern like parler, manger
concepts.example: {je donne}, {tu donnes}, {il donne}, {nous donnons}, {vous donnez}, {ils donnent}

concepts.definition: Give WHAT (direct) to WHOM (indirect) - donner quelque chose à quelqu'un
concepts.example: {Je donne le livre à Marie} (I give the book to Marie) → {Je lui donne le livre} (I give it to her)

concepts.definition: Many fixed phrases use donner in French
concepts.example: {donner l'heure} (tell the time), {donner raison} (agree with someone), {donner rendez-vous} (make an appointment)

concepts.definition: Regular -ER verb for searching - used constantly in daily life
concepts.example: {Je cherche mes clés} (I'm looking for my keys), {Tu cherches quoi?} (What are you looking for?), {C'est dur de trouver mes clés !} (It's hard to find my keys!)

concepts.definition: Regular -ER verb for finding - the successful result of chercher!
concepts.example: {J'ai trouvé!} (I found it!), {Tu trouves ça comment?} (What do you think of that?)

concepts.definition: These two verbs form a natural action sequence
concepts.example: {Je cherche} → {Je trouve} (I search → I find). The complete search-and-discovery process!

concepts.definition: Both verbs have broader meanings beyond physical searching
concepts.example: {chercher} = try to do, {trouver} = think/consider ({Je trouve que...} = I think that...)

concepts.definition: Regular -RE verb for waiting - essential for appointments and transport
concepts.example: {J'attends le bus} (I'm waiting for the bus), {Tu attends quelqu'un?} (Are you waiting for someone?), {J'attends Marie et j'écoute de la musique} (I'm waiting for Marie and listening to music)

concepts.definition: Regular -ER verb for arriving - completing journeys and meetings
concepts.example: {J'arrive à 8h} (I arrive at 8am), {Le train arrive} (The train is arriving)

concepts.definition: Regular -ER verb for staying - not leaving, remaining somewhere

concepts.definition: qu'est-ce qui = what DOES something (subject). qu'est-ce que = what DO you verb (object)

concepts.definition: Use QUI when asking WHAT is doing the action. No other subject after qui!
concepts.example: {Qu'est-ce qui brille?} (What shines?), {Qu'est-ce qui fait du bruit?} (What makes noise?), {Qu'est-ce qui rend l'herbe verte?} (What makes grass green?)

concepts.definition: Use QUE when asking what someone/something DOES TO something. Subject comes after que!
concepts.example: {Qu'est-ce que tu vois?} (What do you see?), {Qu'est-ce que tu manges?} (What are you eating?), {Qu'est-ce que le soleil fait?} (What does the sun do?)

concepts.definition: If 'what' is the subject (no other subject follows) → {qui}. If another subject follows → {que}.
concepts.example: Pattern: [qu'est-ce qui] + [VERB] OR [qu'est-ce que] + [SUBJECT] + [VERB]

concepts.term: Transform ANY Statement into a Question

concepts.example: {Le soleil brille} → {Qu'est-ce qui brille?} (What shines?), {Je vois un oiseau} → {Qu'est-ce que tu vois?} (What do you see?)

mistakes.feedback: Use {qu'est-ce qui} here: 'what' is the subject, and no other subject follows. Use {qu'est-ce que} when another subject follows.

concepts.term: THE KEY DISTINCTION: savoir vs connaître
concepts.definition: savoir = facts/skills (learned), connaître = people/places (familiarity)
concepts.example: {je sais la réponse} (I know the answer) BUT je connais Marie (I know Marie)

concepts.definition: You CANNOT say '{je connais parler}' - use savoir for skills!
concepts.example: ✓ {je sais parler} (I know how to speak), ✗ {je connais parler} (WRONG!)

concepts.definition: Know people, know places, be familiar with things (movies, books, brands)
concepts.example: {je connais ce film} (I know this movie), {tu connais ce restaurant?} (do you know this restaurant?)

concepts.definition: Words that organize speech, show transitions, add emphasis, or fill pauses - natives use them CONSTANTLY!
concepts.example: Without: '{Je ne comprends pas. Je veux apprendre.}' With: '{Bon, je ne comprends pas, donc je veux apprendre, quoi.}' ← Native!

concepts.definition: Shows logical conclusion - very common! Connects cause and effect
concepts.example: {Je pense}, {donc je suis} (I think, therefore I am - Descartes!), {Donc}, {tu comprends?} (So, do you understand?)

concepts.definition: Corrects or clarifies something - super common in conversation
concepts.example: {En fait, je ne sais pas} (Actually, I don't know), {En fait, c'est comme ça} (In fact, that's how it is)

concepts.definition: Filler word - shows hesitation or introduces explanation (informal!)
concepts.example: {Bah, c'est comme ça} (Well, that's how it is), {Bah}, {je sais pas} (Well, I don't know)

concepts.definition: End-of-sentence filler - VERY French! Emphasizes or seeks agreement
concepts.example: {C'est bon}, {quoi} (It's good, you know), {Je pense ça}, quoi (I think that, like)

concepts.definition: bon (well, so), alors (so, then), ainsi (thus - formal)
concepts.example: {Bon}, {on commence?} (Well, shall we start?), {Alors}, {tu viens?} (So, are you coming?), {Alors, tu vas à l'université ? En fait, je n'ai pas de cours aujourd'hui.} (So, are you going to the university? Actually, I don't have class today.), {Bon, voilà la réponse.} (Well, there's the answer.)

concepts.definition: Essential vocabulary for school, university, and learning contexts
concepts.example: {le cours} (class), {la leçon} (lesson), {l'école} (school), {l'université} (university)

concepts.definition: Abstract nouns related to knowing and understanding
concepts.example: {la connaissance} (knowledge - what you know), {le savoir} (knowledge - abstract), {la pensée} (thought)

concepts.definition: Question-and-answer vocabulary - essential for learning!
concepts.example: {la question} (question), {la réponse} (answer), {l'idée} (idea)

concepts.definition: Now you can build full sentences about learning and knowing
concepts.example: {J'ai une question} (I have a question), {C'est une bonne idée} (That's a good idea), {Je vais au cours} (I'm going to class)

concepts.definition: Part of prendre family (you already know this pattern!) - essential for education
concepts.example: {j'apprends le français} (I'm learning French), {j'apprends beaucoup de mots} (I'm learning a lot of words), {nous apprenons ensemble} (we're learning together)

concepts.definition: If you know prendre and comprendre, you know apprendre! Add ap- prefix
concepts.example: {je prends} → {j'apprends}, {tu comprends} → {tu apprends} (same pattern!)

concepts.definition: Regular -ER verb - easy! Natural pair with apprendre
concepts.example: {j'enseigne le français} (I teach French), {il m'enseigne} (he teaches me)

concepts.definition: Teacher teaches → student learns → student understands → student knows
concepts.example: {Il m'enseigne} → {j'apprends} → {je comprends} (complete learning cycle!)

concepts.definition: Use 'à' before infinitive to say learning how to do something
concepts.example: {j'apprends à faire du café} (I'm learning to make coffee), {j'apprends à parler français} (I'm learning to speak French)

concepts.definition: THE most versatile pronoun! Used MORE than '{nous}' in everyday French. Three meanings depending on context.
concepts.example: {on va au cinéma} (we're going to movies), {on va au restaurant en famille} (we're going to a restaurant as a family), {on dit que} (people say that), {on ne peut pas} (one cannot)

concepts.term: on conjugates like il/{elle} (third person singular)
concepts.definition: CRITICAL: Even though '{on}' means 'we', it uses il/elle verb forms!
concepts.example: {on est} (we are), {on a} (we have), {on va} (we go), {on fait} (we do) - all use il/elle forms

concepts.definition: on = informal, conversational (90% of speech). nous = formal, written (10%)
concepts.example: Friends: '{on va manger?}' Formal: '{nous allons manger}' (much less common!)

concepts.definition: Plural noun for referring to people in general - very common!
concepts.example: {les gens disent} (people say), {les gens pensent} (people think), {les gens sont gentils} (people are nice)

concepts.definition: Fixed expression (literally 'all the world') - uses SINGULAR verb!
concepts.example: {tout le monde sait} (everyone knows - singular!), {tout le monde pense} (everyone thinks)

concepts.definition: Use '{on}' for universal truths or common wisdom - sounds philosophical!
concepts.example: {On apprend tous les jours} (We learn every day), {On ne peut pas tout savoir} (One can't know everything)

items/i-on-doit-travailler.hint: on + doit + travailler (on uses il/elle forms)

mistakes.feedback: Use '{on}' for informal - '{on doit travailler}'
'on' takes il/elle forms - '{on doit}' (not 'on devons')!

concepts.definition: Core cognitive verb for expressing opinions and thoughts
concepts.example: {je pense que c'est bon} (I think it's good), {tu penses?} (what do you think?)

concepts.definition: Easy conjugation! Like parler, manger, etc. (verbs you already know)
concepts.example: {je pense}, {tu penses}, {il pense} - add -e, -{es}, -e endings

concepts.definition: Use '{que}' to introduce your opinion - VERY common pattern
concepts.example: {je pense que oui} (I think so), {je pense que non} (I don't think so), {je pense que je connais Marie} (I think I know Marie), {je pense qu'il sait parler anglais} (I think he can speak English)

concepts.definition: Use 'à' + person/thing when thinking about something
concepts.example: {je pense à toi} (I'm thinking about you), {je pense à ça} (I'm thinking about that)

concepts.definition: Qu'est-ce que tu penses? = What do you think? (essential!)
concepts.example: {Qu'est-ce que tu penses de ça?} (What do you think about that?)

concepts.definition: Use savoir + verb to express skills/abilities

concepts.definition: savoir = facts/skills, connaître = people/places (you'll learn connaître next!)

concepts.definition: In positive commands, pronouns attach to the verb with hyphens
concepts.example: {Donne-le!} (Give it!), {Regarde-moi!} (Look at me!), {Écoute-le!} (Listen to him!), {Regarde-moi et fais attention!} (Look at me and pay attention!), {Amuse-toi bien!} (Have fun!), {Dépêche-toi, habille-toi!} (Hurry up, get dressed!)

concepts.definition: In negative commands, pronouns go BEFORE the verb (normal position)
concepts.example: {Ne le fais pas!} (Don't do it!), {Ne me regarde pas!} (Don't look at me!)

concepts.definition: Object pronouns: le/la/les come first, then moi/toi
concepts.example: {Donne-le-moi!} (Give it to me! - le before moi), {Montre-la-moi!} (Show it to me!)

concepts.definition: {en} stands for something you already named with {du}, {de la}, {de l'}, {des} or a number. In a statement it goes before the verb. In a positive command it goes after the verb, with a hyphen, like the other pronouns.
concepts.example: {Tu veux du café ? Oui, j'en veux.} (Do you want some coffee? Yes, I want some.), {Prends-en !} (Take some!)

concepts.definition: Tell someone to do something - no subject pronoun needed!
concepts.example: {Mange!} (Eat!), {Parle!} (Speak!), {Va!} (Go!), {Pars tôt!} (Leave early!)

concepts.term: tu form: Just Drop the Pronoun!
concepts.definition: For most verbs, use the tu form without '{tu}'
concepts.example: {tu manges} → {Mange!} (you eat → Eat!), {tu parles} → {Parle!} (you speak → Speak!)

concepts.definition: For -ER verbs only, also drop the final -s in tu command form
concepts.example: {tu manges} → {Mange!} (not Manges!), {tu parles} → {Parle!} (not Parles!)

concepts.definition: tu commands are informal - use with people you'd call '{tu}'
concepts.example: To a friend: {Mange!} (Eat!), {Écoute!} (Listen!), {Viens!} (Come!), {Viens, on est en retard!} (Come on, we're late!)

concepts.definition: Use vous form for strangers, bosses, or multiple people
concepts.example: To strangers: Mangez! To a group: {Venez ! On se voit demain !} (Come! See you tomorrow!)

concepts.definition: Just use vous form without saying '{vous}'
concepts.example: {vous mangez} → {Mangez!}, {vous parlez} → {Parlez!}

concepts.definition: Unlike tu commands, vous commands keep all letters!
concepts.example: {Mangez!} (not Mange!), {Parlez!} (not Parle!)

concepts.definition: Regular -IR verb for sleeping - essential for daily routines
concepts.example: {je dors} (I sleep), {je dors huit heures} (I sleep 8 hours), {tu dors bien?} (do you sleep well?)

concepts.definition: Regular -ER verb for working - essential for adult life
concepts.example: {je travaille} (I work), {je travaille à Paris} (I work in Paris), {où travaillez-vous?} (where do you work?)

concepts.definition: Irregular verb for living/being alive - existential and location
concepts.example: {je vis} (I live), {je vis à Paris} (I live in Paris), {vivre sa vie} (to live one's life)

concepts.definition: These three verbs complete your ability to describe human existence
concepts.example: {Je vis à Paris, je travaille près d'ici, et je dors bien} (I live in Paris, work near here, and sleep well)

concepts.definition: Recall memories - important mental action
concepts.example: {je me souviens de ça} (I remember that), {tu te souviens?} (do you remember?)

concepts.term: {s'amuser} = to have fun / to enjoy oneself
concepts.definition: Enjoying yourself - social/emotional
concepts.example: {je m'amuse} (I'm having fun), {on s'amuse bien} (we're having a good time)

concepts.definition: Moving quickly - time pressure!
concepts.example: {je me dépêche} (I'm hurrying), {je me dépêche, je suis en retard} (I'm hurrying, I'm late), {dépêche-toi!} (hurry up!)

concepts.definition: Personal hygiene - wash yourself

concepts.definition: Put clothes on yourself - daily essential!

concepts.definition: General preparation - for school, work, going out

mistakes.feedback: Close! But '{grâce à}' + noun is more elegant than 'parce que' + clause here.
Succeeding is positive! Use '{grâce à}' for positive attribution.

items/i-parce-que-2.text: Pourquoi tu ne viens pas ? - ___ je suis fatigué
items/i-parce-que-2.gloss: Why aren't you coming? - Because I'm tired

mistakes.feedback: Car works but sounds formal. Use '{parce que}' to answer '{pourquoi}'.
Puisque is for known facts, not direct answers to '{pourquoi}'. Use '{parce que}'!

items/i-puisque-2.text: On va partir ___ tu es là

mistakes.feedback: Parce que works! But '{puisque}' emphasizes the logical conclusion better.
Car works but '{puisque}' is more natural for 'since'.

items/i-etais-2.text: Quand j'___ jeune, je jouais avec mon chien
items/i-etais-2.gloss: When I was young, I used to play with my dog

mistakes.feedback: That's passé composé! Use imparfait for description: j'étais jeune.
That's present tense! Use imparfait: j'étais (I was).
That's il/elle form! Use '{je}' form: j'étais (not était).

vocabulary/je-jouais-fr.gloss: I was playing / I used to play

concepts.definition: Indicates proximity, nearness
concepts.example: {Le café est près de l'école} (The café is near the school), {J'habite près d'ici} (I live near here)

concepts.definition: Indicates distance, remoteness
concepts.example: {La gare est loin de la maison} (The station is far from the house), {C'est loin d'ici?} (Is it far from here?)

concepts.definition: Indicates immediate proximity, side-by-side position
concepts.example: {Je suis à côté de toi} (I'm next to you), {Le restaurant est à côté du cinéma} (The restaurant is next to the cinema)

concepts.definition: Indicates facing position, directly opposite
concepts.example: {Ma maison est en face du parc} (My house is across from the park), {Il est assis en face de moi} (He's sitting across from me)

concepts.definition: Indicates surrounding position
concepts.example: {Les gens sont autour de la table} (People are around the table), {Autour de la ville} (Around the city)

concepts.definition: Indicates position along a length
concepts.example: {Le long de la rue} (Along the street), {On marche le long de la rivière} (We walk along the river)

concepts.term: {au milieu de} - in the middle of
concepts.definition: Indicates center position
concepts.example: {Au milieu de la place} (In the middle of the square), {Il est au milieu} (He's in the middle)

concepts.term: {au bout de} - at the end of
concepts.definition: Indicates end position
concepts.example: {Au bout de la rue} (At the end of the street), {C'est au bout} (It's at the end)

mistakes.feedback: Avec means 'with'. Use '{à côté de}' for physical position 'next to'!
Près de means 'near' (general). Use '{à côté de}' for 'right next to'!

items/i-au-bout-du.gloss: The door is at the end of the garden

mistakes.feedback: Dans means 'in' (general). Use '{au bout de}' for 'at the end of'!
Près de means 'near'. Use '{au bout de}' for 'at the end of'!

items/i-au-milieu-de-la.gloss: The table is in the middle of the kitchen

mistakes.feedback: Dans means 'in' (general). Use '{au milieu de}' for 'in the middle of'!
Sur means 'on'. Use '{au milieu de}' for 'in the middle of'!

items/i-sont-rentres.gloss: Paul and Marc came home late

mistakes.feedback: Paul et Marc is plural! Add -s for masculine plural: {sont rentrés}.
Paul and Marc are men, so use -s (not -es): {sont rentrés}.
Rentrer uses ÊTRE, not avoir! It's '{sont rentrés}', not 'ont rentrés'.

vocabulary/vous-etes-alle-fr.note: formal singular masculine; masculine singular (no change)

vocabulary/vous-etes-alles-fr.example_fr: Les enfants, vous êtes allés où ?

concepts.definition: Compound past tense for completed actions: auxiliary verb '{avoir}' + past participle
concepts.example: {j'ai parlé} (I spoke), {tu as mangé} (you ate), {il a étudié} (he studied)

concepts.definition: Remove -er, add -é: parler → parlé, manger → mangé, étudier → étudié
concepts.example: {parler} → {parlé} (spoken), {manger} → {mangé} (eaten), {aimer} → {aimé} (loved)

concepts.definition: Use present tense of avoir + past participle ending in -é
concepts.example: {j'ai parlé}, {tu as parlé}, {il}/{elle a parlé}, {nous avons parlé}, {vous avez parlé}, {ils}/{elles ont parlé}

concepts.definition: Place ne and pas around the auxiliary verb avoir
concepts.example: {je n'ai pas parlé} (I didn't speak), {tu n'as pas mangé} (you didn't eat)

concepts.definition: Invert avoir with subject, or use est-ce que
concepts.example: {As-tu parlé?} (Did you speak?), {Est-ce que tu as mangé?} (Did you eat?)

concepts.definition: For specific completed actions in the past, countable events
concepts.example: {Hier, j'ai parlé avec Marie} (Yesterday, I spoke with Marie), {J'ai mangé à 8h} (I ate at 8)

items/i-a-regarde.gloss: We watched a film last night

mistakes.feedback: That's present tense! Use passé composé: on a regardé (we watched).
Change -er to -é! The past participle is '{regardé}', not 'regarder'.

items/i-avez-cherche.gloss: Did you look for my book?

mistakes.feedback: That's present tense! Use passé composé: vous avez cherché (you looked for).
Change -er to -é! The past participle is '{cherché}', not 'chercher'.
'Avons' is for '{nous}'! Use '{avez}' for vous: vous avez cherché.
Venir uses ÊTRE! Use '{elle n'est pas venue}', not 'a pas venu'.
That's present tense! Use passé composé: elle n'est pas venue.

items/i-etes-entres.gloss: Did you go into the café?

mistakes.feedback: Entrer uses ÊTRE, not avoir! Use '{êtes-vous entrés ?}' (motion verb).
That's present tense! Use passé composé: {êtes-vous entrés ?}
Rester uses ÊTRE, not avoir! Use '{vous êtes restés}' (a DR & MRS VANDERTRAMP verb).
That's present tense! Use passé composé: {vous êtes restés}.

vocabulary/elle-est-venue-ils-sont-venus.fr: elle est venue / ils sont venus
vocabulary/elle-est-venue-ils-sont-venus.note: with être the ending agrees: -e for feminine, -s for plural

vocabulary/il-est-ne-il-est-mort-fr.fr: il est né / il est mort
vocabulary/il-est-ne-il-est-mort-fr.note: naître → né, mourir → mort (both use être!)

concepts.definition: Irregular past participle: j'ai eu, tu as eu, il a eu
concepts.example: {J'ai eu le temps} (I had time), {J'ai eu de la chance} (I had luck/I was lucky)

concepts.definition: Irregular past participle: j'ai été, tu as été, il a été
concepts.example: {J'ai été content} (I was happy), {J'ai été à Paris} (I went to Paris - informal)

concepts.definition: Irregular past participle: j'ai fait, tu as fait, il a fait
concepts.example: {J'ai fait ça} (I did that), {J'ai fait mes devoirs} (I did my homework), {J'ai fait un gâteau} (I made a cake)

concepts.definition: Irregular past participle: j'ai vu, tu as vu, il a vu
concepts.example: {J'ai vu le film} (I saw the movie), {Tu as vu Marie?} (Did you see Marie?), {J'ai vu Paul, il est assis au café} (I saw Paul, he's sitting at the café)

concepts.definition: These 4 verbs are the most common - memorize them!
concepts.example: {eu}, {été}, {fait}, {vu} - practice these until automatic

concepts.definition: These 4 verbs all use '{avoir}' (not être) in passé composé
concepts.example: {j'ai eu}, {j'ai été}, {j'ai fait}, {j'ai vu} (all with '{avoir}')

concepts.definition: Combine: 1) Scene-setting (IMP), 2) Events (PC), 3) Causal reasoning (parce que, car), 4) Spatial context (près de, devant)
concepts.example: {Hier, il faisait beau donc je suis allé au parc près de chez moi. J'étais content parce que j'avais du temps.}

concepts.definition: Background (IMP) → Event (PC) → Reason (parce que) → Next Event (PC)
concepts.example: {Il faisait beau} (background) {quand je suis sorti} (event). {J'ai décidé d'aller au café} (event) {parce que j'avais faim} (reason).

concepts.definition: Use spatial prepositions + imparfait to paint the picture
concepts.example: {Le café était près de l'école. Il y avait beaucoup de gens. Ils étaient assis autour des tables.}

concepts.definition: Use donc, parce que, car, comme to connect events logically
concepts.example: {Comme il faisait beau, je suis sorti. J'ai vu Marie donc on a parlé. On est allés au café car on avait faim.}

concepts.definition: Combine temporal words (d'abord, ensuite) with spatial (près de, devant)
concepts.example: {D'abord, je suis allé au café près de l'école. Ensuite, j'ai vu Marie devant le cinéma. Après, j'ai joué avec mon chien.}

items/i-a-cause-de.text: ___ la fête, on est rentrés tard
items/i-a-cause-de.gloss: Because of the party, we got home late

mistakes.feedback: The party is the cause here, not a thanks. Use '{à cause de}'.
Use '{à cause de la fête}' (because of THE PARTY, a noun).

items/i-ai-fait-ensuite.text: J'___ mes devoirs ___ j'ai écouté de la musique
items/i-ai-fait-ensuite.gloss: I did my homework then I listened to music

mistakes.feedback: Completed homework = specific event! Use passé composé: j'ai fait.
'Car' is for reason! Use '{ensuite}' (then) for sequence.

items/i-grace-a.gloss: Thanks to you, I learned French

mistakes.feedback: Parce que needs a CLAUSE! Use '{Grâce à toi}' (thanks to you - NOUN).
Succeeding is POSITIVE! Use '{grâce à}' (not à cause de which is negative/neutral).

items/i-j-en-ai-mange.text: Il y avait du pain, alors j'en ___.
items/i-j-en-ai-mange.gloss: There was some bread, so I ate some.

mistakes.feedback: Eating the bread is the event, so use the passé composé: {j'en ai mangé}.

items/i-parce-que.gloss: Because I was hungry, I ate

mistakes.feedback: Grâce à is POSITIVE and needs a NOUN! Use '{Parce que}' + clause for hunger.
À cause de needs a NOUN! Use '{Parce que j'avais faim}' (because I was hungry).

items/i-sur-dans.text: Le livre était ___ la table ___ la cuisine
items/i-sur-dans.gloss: The book was on the table in the kitchen

mistakes.feedback: Wrong order! The book is ON (sur) the table, IN (dans) the room.
Au-dessus means 'above' (hanging). Use '{sur}' for '{on}' (touching surface).

concepts.definition: PASSÉ COMPOSÉ = Specific completed action (What happened?). IMPARFAIT = Ongoing state/description/habit (How things were/used to be)
concepts.example: {J'ai mangé} (I ate - specific event) vs Je mangeais (I was eating/used to eat - ongoing or habit)

concepts.definition: Completed actions, countable events, things that started/stopped, main storyline
concepts.example: {J'ai vu Marie} (I saw Marie - one time), {Je suis allé au café} (I went to the café - completed)

concepts.definition: Descriptions, ongoing states, repeated habits ('used to'), scene-setting, background information
concepts.example: {Il faisait beau} (It was nice - description), {Je parlais français tous les jours} (I used to speak French every day - habit)

concepts.definition: Use imparfait to set the scene, passé composé for what happened
concepts.example: {Il faisait beau} (background - IMP) {quand je suis arrivé} (event - PC) = It was nice when I arrived

concepts.definition: PC: hier (yesterday), soudain (suddenly), à 8h (at 8). IMP: tous les jours (every day), toujours (always), d'habitude (usually)
concepts.example: {Hier}, {j'ai mangé} (PC - specific time) vs Je mangeais tous les jours (IMP - habit)

concepts.definition: Use imparfait for ongoing action, passé composé for interruption
concepts.example: {Je parlais avec Marie} (I was talking - IMP) {quand tu as appelé} (you called - PC event)

concepts.definition: Physical age/description = IMP. Mental state at moment = can be PC
concepts.example: {J'avais 20 ans} (I was 20 - IMP description) vs J'ai eu peur (I got scared - {PC reaction})

items/i-jouais.text: Quand j'étais jeune, je ___ avec mon chien
items/i-jouais.gloss: When I was young, I used to play with my dog

mistakes.feedback: Repeated past action (habit)! Use imparfait: je jouais (I used to play).
That's present! Use imparfait for past habit: je jouais.

items/i-prenais-un-cafe.text: Je ___ un café quand tu es arrivé
items/i-prenais-un-cafe.gloss: I was having a coffee when you arrived

mistakes.feedback: Ongoing action (was having)! Use imparfait: je prenais.
That's present! Use imparfait for ongoing past: je prenais.

vocabulary/je-mangeais-fr.gloss: I was eating / I used to eat

concepts.term: Reflexive Verbs ALWAYS use être in Past
concepts.definition: CRITICAL: ALL reflexive verbs use être (never avoir) in passé composé
concepts.example: {je me suis lavé} (I washed myself - uses être), {elle s'est levée} (she got up - uses être)

concepts.definition: Past participle agrees with the subject (like all être verbs)
concepts.example: {je me suis réveillé} (masc), {je me suis réveillée} (fem), {ils se sont levés} (masc pl), {elles se sont levées} (fem pl)

concepts.definition: Reflexive pronoun stays BEFORE the auxiliary être
concepts.example: {je me suis levé} (not je suis me levé), {tu t'es lavé} (not tu es te lavé)

concepts.definition: Now you can describe what you did this morning!
concepts.example: {Ce matin, je me suis réveillé à 7h. Ensuite, je me suis levé. Après, je me suis lavé. J'étais en retard, donc je me suis dépêché.}

concepts.definition: Indicates position in front of something
concepts.example: {Je suis devant la porte} (I'm in front of the door), {La voiture est devant la maison} (The car is in front of the house)

concepts.definition: Indicates position behind something
concepts.example: {Le chat est derrière le sofa} (The cat is behind the sofa), {Il est derrière moi} (He's behind me)

concepts.definition: Indicates position between two things
concepts.example: {Le café est entre l'école et le parc} (The café is between the school and the park), {Entre toi et moi} (Between you and me)

concepts.definition: Indicates being among multiple things or people
concepts.example: {Parmi les étudiants} (Among the students), {Il est parmi nous} (He's among us)

concepts.definition: Indicates position above something
concepts.example: {Le tableau est au-dessus de la table} (The painting is above the table), {Au-dessus de la ville} (Above the city)

concepts.definition: Indicates position below something
concepts.example: {au-dessous de nous} (below us), {Le parking est au-dessous} (The parking is below)

concepts.definition: Reinforce: dans (in/inside), sur (on/on top of), sous (under/beneath)
concepts.example: {Le livre est dans le sac} (in the bag), {sur la table} (on the table), {sous la table} (under the table)

mistakes.feedback: Au-dessus means 'above/upstairs'. Use '{au-dessous}' for 'below/downstairs'!
En bas works too! But we're learning '{au-dessous}' here.
Use '{au-dessus de}' for 'above'.
Devant means 'in front of'. Use '{au-dessus de}' for 'above'!

items/i-sous-2.gloss: The cat is under the car

mistakes.feedback: Sur means 'on top of'. Use '{sous}' for 'under/beneath'!
Dans means 'in/inside'. Use '{sous}' for 'under/beneath'!

items/i-sur.gloss: My phone is on the table

mistakes.feedback: Dans means 'in/inside'. Use '{sur}' for 'on top of' a surface!
Au-dessus means 'above' (not touching). Use '{sur}' for '{on}' (touching)!

parts/p-keep-the-article.heading: Keep the article
text: Every French noun is masculine or feminine, so learn each cognate with its article, {un} or {une}. French does not drop the article the way English does in “Coffee is good”.
parts/p-keep-the-article.note: Every time you recognize a cognate, you add a French word without studying it.

concepts.definition: Very common verb for giving things, offering help, providing information
concepts.example: {je donne le livre} (I give the book), {tu donnes ton nom} (you give your name)

concepts.definition: Present tense: je donne, tu donnes, il donne, nous donnons, vous donnez, ils donnent
concepts.example: Regular pattern: donn- + endings (-e, -{es}, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent)

concepts.definition: Giving objects (donner un cadeau), giving information (donner l'adresse), giving help (donner de l'aide)
concepts.example: {je donne mon numéro} (I give my number), {ça donne faim} (it makes you hungry)

concepts.definition: Perfect opposites - donner (to give) and prendre (to take)
concepts.example: {je donne le livre à Marie, elle prend le livre} (I give the book to Marie, she takes the book)

concepts.definition: Often used with 'à' (to) - donner quelque chose à quelqu'un
concepts.example: {je donne le livre à mon ami} (I give the book to my friend)

concepts.definition: {rien} takes the place of {pas}: {ne} goes before the verb and {rien} after it.
concepts.example: {Il ne donne rien.} (He doesn't give anything.), {Je ne vois rien.} (I don't see anything.)

mistakes.feedback: For nothing, {rien} takes the place of {pas}: {il ne dit rien}.
For nothing, {rien} takes the place of {pas}: {il ne donne rien}.

items/i-je-ne-fais-rien.situation: A friend asks {Qu'est-ce que tu fais ?} Say you're not doing anything.

mistakes.feedback: People often drop {ne} when they speak, but write it here: {je ne fais rien}.

accept: je ne fais rien du tout

mistakes.feedback: {rien} takes the place of {pas}: {je ne vois rien}.

concepts.definition: Active searching - when you're looking for something but haven't found it yet
concepts.example: {je cherche mon livre} (I'm looking for my book), {tu cherches quoi?} (what are you looking for?)

concepts.definition: Successfully locating something - the result of searching
concepts.example: {j'ai trouvé!} (I found it!), {tu trouves ça où?} (where do you find that?)

concepts.definition: These verbs are used constantly in daily French conversation
concepts.example: je cherche + noun (I'm looking for...), je trouve + noun (I find...)

concepts.definition: chercher takes direct objects, trouver can use various prepositions
concepts.example: {je cherche le livre} (I'm looking for the book), {je trouve dans la maison} (I find in the house)

checks.ask: Which one means “I don't have a cat”?

options.text: Je ne ai pas de chat.

checks.why: After {pas}, {un} becomes {de}, and {ne} becomes {n'} before a vowel: {Je n'ai pas de chat.}

checks.ask: Which one means “You aren't a child”?

options.text: Tu ne pas es un enfant.

checks.why: {ne} goes before the verb and {pas} after it. After {être}, {un} stays as it is: {Tu n'es pas un enfant.}

checks.ask: Which one means “I don't have a car anymore”?
checks.why: {plus} takes the place of {pas} and means anymore.
